extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent prosecutors, USPTO policymakers, and IP scholars/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended procedural rules for improving public notice and claim clarity during patent prosecution (examiner behavior, applicant disclosures, specification content, and standards of examination). Focused on U.S. patent prosecution practice and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject vague or indefinite claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should reject vague claim language and force more definite and unambiguous expressions of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 35 U.S.C. § 112, examiners have statutory authority to reject applications that do not completely and unambiguously describe and enable the claimed invention. Increasing rejections on this ground will incentivize applicants to clarify initial applications (because specification changes can constitute new matter and affect priority). Example/anti-pattern: permitting claims that cover both patentable and non-patentable subject matter (Prater) leads to invalid claims; examiners should notify patentees when claims are too broad and require narrowing (e.g., limit to digital computers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners require disclaimers and applicant definitions when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an applicant explains that certain prior art does not apply or asserts a specific meaning for a term, the examiner should require a clear disclaimer or require that the definition be reflected in the claims or specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring disclaimers or explicit definitions creates a clearer public record and allows courts to apply disclaimers when construing claims (SanDisk v. Memorex). Trademark practice provides an analogy (examiners routinely require disclaimers for non-protectable words). If definitions or disclaimers are ambiguous, courts will not use them to limit ordinary meaning. Examples: require a disclaimer when applicant distinguishes prior art; require that a declared meaning of a term be placed into the claims or specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should take an active role and issue 'reasons for allowance' statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should compile and state the reasons why particular claims were allowed—documenting which limitations made a claim allowable over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A final 'reasons for allowance' document would explain that a claim was allowed because it included a certain limitation (enhances public notice). If binding on courts, such a document would further improve claim construction consistency. This proposal relies on examiners already knowing reasons for allowance and would not significantly lengthen review if done succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should police word/phrase interpretation during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should actively identify ambiguities, explore scope and breadth of language, and impose clarification during prosecution rather than leaving ambiguities unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP and caselaw (In re Zletz) encourage recognition and clarification of ambiguities during prosecution. Doing so increases public notice by producing clearer claim language or explicit disclaimers/definitions in the record. This may involve affirmative statements about the examiner's understanding of what the patent is and is not intended to cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require examiners to create full claim charts for every application
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not be required to prepare detailed claim charts for every patent application because of the substantial time cost relative to public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating proper claim charts can take hours or days; with ~4,000 examiners and ~400,000 applications per year, requiring claim charts would impose significant workload increases (even 30 extra minutes each is meaningful). Only a small percentage of patents are litigated, and even then only a subset of claim terms are disputed, so requiring full claim charts is inefficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require a comprehensive lexicon for every patent; require targeted definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should not be forced to provide a complete lexicon defining every word in every claim, because such a requirement is costly and still leaves ambiguity; instead, require definitions or clarifying amendments for terms likely to be disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full lexicon for a patent with many claims could require hundreds of definitions and spawn disputes over definitions themselves. Targeted definition requirements—where examiners or applicants identify specific disputed terms and place definitions in the patent—are more cost-effective and improve notice for the terms most likely to be litigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce written description and enablement requirements (35 U.S.C. § 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should more vigorously reject applications that fail to provide sufficient detail in the written specification to describe and enable the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger enforcement of § 112 will incentivize applicants to produce comprehensive initial specifications, which clarify claim meaning and reduce reliance on prosecution history. Rejecting ill-described applications prevents applicants from using vague claims to obtain unwarranted scope, and because changes to the specification can be new matter, applicants prefer priority and therefore will supply better initial detail. Example: Eli Lilly/regents case where insufficient description invalidated overbroad claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require detailed description of preferred embodiments and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should be required (or examiners should insist) to provide more detail on how the invention is implemented in preferred embodiments to clarify what is and is not part of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear preferred-embodiment descriptions help courts construe ambiguous terms (Globetrotter: specification showed 'preventing' included passive 'no-license' messages). Applicants may resist for fear of limiting claim scope (Honeywell), so examiner pressure is necessary. Marginal cost of accurate descriptions is likely low since applicants understand their inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require applicants to include a description of the prior art and preferred reference sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications should include a section describing the applicant’s understanding of the known prior art and listing preferred reference sources that the applicant relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disclosure helps surface unwritten or obscure background information, gives examiners and readers a baseline for comparison, clarifies terms in light of the state of the art, and helps courts assess the ordinary skill level at filing time. Risks: applicants might strategically omit or misstate prior art, but duty of candor and inequitable conduct risk mitigates this. This proposal does not mandate a prior art search but asks for the applicant's understanding of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relax the obviousness standard to allow more prior art to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure adequate testing of claims against prior art, the obviousness standard should be relaxed (as KSR did) so examiners can consider more prior art and combinations when evaluating patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoning the broadest reasonable construction rule risks narrower prosecution-stage interpretations that exclude relevant prior art; relaxing obviousness helps preserve substantive examination against as much relevant prior art as possible. Prior Federal Circuit tests requiring explicit teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine limited examiners' ability to find combinations; KSR's approach permits broader consideration of prior art combination to test validity and define outer claim limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit and encourage examiner-initiated amendments to improve clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should be empowered to amend patent applications or require applicant amendments (e.g., to add disclaimers or definitions) when necessary to obtain clear claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.121(g) and MPEP § 714(II)(E)) already provide for examiner amendments, though they are rarely used; encouraging such amendments would reverse the trend of applicant-initiated-only amendments and could efficiently produce clearer claims without requiring wholesale new disclosure from applicants. Applicants who disagree can respond and attempt to clarify their intent.
